5. CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

The study has demonstrated that horizontal drains can be effective in
reducing tne water taple at Po Shan. Drains 46, H7 and 88 lowered the
water table by over 3.0 m at a distance of 10 m from the drain group. A
scheme comprising several rows of drains can be expected to produce
appreciably larger drawdowns than these three isolated drains.

Tne available methods for the design of horizontal drainage schemes
contain certain simplifications which make their applicability suspect.
Some design methods use two-dimensional analysis, which may be invalid
unless the drain spacing is small. The three-dimensional design methods
take no account of the effective hydraulic drain radius. In addition, any
design method needs to take account of infiltration, as this will lead to
a significant rise in groundwater levels downstream of any system of
horizontal drains,

The main problems associated witn any systen of long horizontal
drains will be those associated with the drilling of long enough holes and
with tne installation of the drain liners. ‘The drilling methods adopted
need to safeguard against nole collapse in order to avoid loosening the
soil over large areas of the nillside. To ensure tnat the nole does not
collapse, casing should not be withdrawn beneath the water table in soil
until after tne installation of the drain liner. To be able to comply
witn this requirement in holes greater than 70 m in length, 'down-the—
hole' hammers and under-reaming oits are required. Any contractor
undertaking such work must have a variety of sucn drilling options
available, because difficulties are invariably encountered. Only by
having flexipility to change between alternative drilling methods can
these be overcome. ‘The drilling macninery itselr inust be of high pullout
capacity and torque, yet be light enougn to be moved between holes
easily. Tnis can pest pe acnieved py tne use of feed pean drills
with separate hydraulic power packs.

Drain liner installation poses problems pelow the water table. It is
concluded fron the trials that a supstantial clearance between drain liner
and casing must be maintained to prevent soil particles from jamming them
together. Alternatively, a minimal clearance could perhaps be used in
conjunction witn some form of ‘wiper’, so that any gap is too small to
allow soil particles to enter the annulus. ‘Tine drain liner must pe of
sufficient strength to prevent breakage under the forces experienced
during installation. Stainless steel is recommended as being the most
suitasle material, pecause it has high strength and is corrosion
resistant.

There is little evidence to indicate that drain performance at Po
Snan will deteriorate with time due to screen clogging. Chemical tests on
samples of groundwater have been carried out, and these have not
identified any compounds likely to clog the screen by precipitation.
Also, tne literature does not generally consider clogging to pe a major
problem, as long as the groundwater does not contain substances that will
precipitate onto tne screen. A regular programme of maintenance must be
implemented to clear vegetation growth from around drain outlets to
prevent tnis from reducing drain performance.
